title: Reading the Dark
paragraphs: Every telescope is, in a sense, a time machine, but the James Webb Space Telescope makes that claim unusually literal. Launched on Christmas Day in two thousand twenty one, it now orbits near the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point, roughly one and a half million kilometres from Earth, where the combined gravity of the two bodies lets it hold a stable position economically. Its purpose is to collect infrared light from objects so distant that their radiation has been travelling for billions of years.

Infrared observation demands extreme thermal discipline, since warmth from the instrument itself would drown out the faint signals it is built to detect. That requirement helps explain both the remote orbit and the delicate engineering of the observatory. Its primary mirror, about six and a half metres wide, is assembled from eighteen hexagonal segments coated with gold, and the segments are aligned so precisely that they function as a single surface.

Collecting light, however, is only the beginning of the scientific labour. A faint smear of infrared radiation does not announce its own meaning; astronomers must infer distance, age and composition from patterns in the signal, each inference resting on models that can themselves be revised. Early results from any new instrument therefore tend to provoke vigorous disagreement before they settle into consensus.

That disagreement should not be mistaken for failure. On the contrary, it is the ordinary mechanism by which a new kind of evidence is tested against existing theory. A telescope that only confirmed what astronomers already believed would be a poor investment, however magnificent its mirror.

What Webb ultimately offers is not a finished picture of the early universe but a better set of questions. Whether those questions will be answered within a decade or a generation remains uncertain, and honest accounts of the mission acknowledge as much. Looking further has rarely produced simpler answers; it has usually produced better arguments.
